cycles.en_text_before_rewrite:
# The AI Phone Call Had a Human Helper

An AI called. That was what people thought as they spoke. But a human appeared from behind the scenes. A test involving Muse, Meta’s AI agent, became a reveal of what was really happening.

### The human backup plan

Through Muse, trained human contract workers made some calls and completed the exchanges with users. The idea was practical: when AI struggled, a person could help. Keeping a human in reserve seemed safer than leaving everything to AI.

But that backup plan changed the meaning of the call.

### The hidden cost of a smooth call

The test began without properly telling people what was happening. So people who thought they were speaking with AI were actually speaking with human staff. These workers did more than make the conversation smooth: the user’s sensitive information might be shared with contract workers at a call center. One helper meant one more person handling private data.

This is the interesting, slightly frightening turn. People often worry that an AI phone call will produce a strange answer. Here, the opposite happened. The voice was not simply human-like; a human was really speaking. And people were not properly told.

In response, a Meta executive admitted that starting a test in which contract workers made calls without properly telling people was a mistake. The human concierge feature was then rolled back for the time being.

AI stories usually focus on machines moving closer to people. Muse asks a different question: if humans enter AI’s backstage, can users be told? Who is speaking, and who can see the information?

## In one line

Unless both facts are explained at the start, a service of the future can quickly look like a call from a stranger.

deviations.claim_in_article: “when AI struggled, a person could help” and “Keeping a human in reserve seemed safer than leaving everything to AI.”
deviations.issue: The Ledger confirms that trained human contractors handled some Muse calls, but does not establish that they were used as a backup when AI struggled or that this was the reason for the test. The article presents that rationale as an interpretation, but it adds an unsupported explanation for the arrangement.
deviations.explanation: The backup rationale and link to AI struggling are not established by the Ledger; the conditional wording softens the claim but does not supply evidence for it.
same_fact_id_locations: The human backup plan — “when AI struggled, a person could help”

deviations.claim_in_article: “These workers did more than make the conversation smooth”
deviations.issue: The Ledger says the human contractors made calls and completed exchanges, but does not report that they made the conversations smooth. The article adds an unverified description of the calls’ quality.
deviations.explanation: The claim that the conversations were smooth is not in the Ledger; it goes beyond the reported fact that contractors completed the exchanges.
same_fact_id_locations: The hidden cost of a smooth call — “These workers did more than make the conversation smooth”

deviations.claim_in_article: “The human backup plan” and “that backup plan” characterize the human-staff calls as a backup arrangement.
deviations.issue: The Ledger confirms that trained contractors handled some calls, but does not establish that they were positioned as a backup or fallback. The Japanese source already uses this framing.
deviations.explanation: The article adds an unverified backup-role characterization; changed_fact and unsupported_new_claim are true.
same_fact_id_locations: Section heading: “The human backup plan”
Sentence: “But that backup plan changed the meaning of the call.”

deviations.claim_in_article: “That was what people thought as they spoke” and “people who thought they were speaking with AI were actually speaking with human staff.”
deviations.issue: The Ledger supports that some calls were made by human contractors and that the test lacked appropriate disclosure, but does not establish that recipients believed they were speaking with AI. The article also links that belief to the lack of disclosure.
deviations.explanation: The recipients’ belief is asserted as fact, generalized beyond the documented observation, and causally linked to nondisclosure without support; the Japanese source already makes this inference.
same_fact_id_locations: Opening paragraph: “That was what people thought as they spoke.”
Paragraph beginning “The test began without properly telling people what was happening”: “So people who thought they were speaking with AI were actually speaking with human staff.”
